name: Regression Test & Live Behavior Guard
sprintRole: Prove that a change preserves previously accepted behavior while adding or repairing the requested behavior, using impact-guided automated regressions plus canonical live tests when the claim is runtime-facing
useWhen: A code, configuration, migration, refactor, bug fix, or feature change may break behavior that previously worked, especially when agents are tempted to validate only the new happy path or the tests they just edited.
inspectFirst: Current default-branch fixed point; exact changed head/diff; original user outcome and prior accepted behavior; existing tests and runtime evidence; callers/call stacks/interfaces/contracts/state boundaries touched by the change; incidents and regressions; canonical launchers/entrypoints; safe live-test environment and proof limits.
expectedOutput: A protected-behavior ledger, change-impact/call-stack map, before/after regression evidence, new and existing automated tests, canonical live behavior proof when safely available, repaired regressions, deliberate second-pass review, and an honest proof ceiling for any runtime that cannot be exercised.
nextStep: Pin the known-good fixed point and changed head, derive the smallest protected-behavior set from accepted behavior and impacted call stacks, run baseline/current tests plus the canonical live path where safe, repair any regression without weakening the old contract, then rerun both old and new behavior through a second pass.
proofGate: Previously accepted behavior is explicit rather than inferred from the changed tests alone; impacted callers/call stacks and state/contracts are inspected; expected outputs are not rewritten merely to bless a regression; both requested behavior and protected controls pass; runtime-facing claims receive canonical live proof when safely executable or an exact runtime blocker/proof ceiling; and a deliberate second pass finds no practical untested regression surface in scope.
copyContent:
PROVE THIS CHANGE DID NOT BREAK BEHAVIOR THAT ALREADY WORKED. TEST THE NEW OUTCOME AND THE PROTECTED OLD OUTCOMES; DO NOT VALIDATE ONLY THE PATH YOU JUST CHANGED.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Change / PR / commit: xyz_change_identity
Requested outcome: xyz_new_or_repaired_behavior
Known-good reference: resolve current accepted main/release/commit from evidence

MISSION
Treat regression testing as preservation proof. Establish what was already expected to keep working, determine which call stacks/contracts/state transitions the change can affect, exercise the smallest meaningful protected set before and after the change when practical, and repair any breakage without weakening the old contract just to make tests green. For runtime-facing use cases, run the canonical live path yourself when a safe environment is available.

1. PIN THE COMPARISON FLOOR
- Refresh repository/provider truth and identify the exact known-good reference and exact candidate head.
- Preserve versioned evidence: a test or live run proves only the head, inputs, environment, and entrypoint it actually observed.
- If the reference itself is already broken or ambiguous, say so and use the strongest earlier accepted evidence rather than fabricating a baseline.

2. BUILD THE PROTECTED-BEHAVIOR LEDGER
Recover behavior that the change must preserve from:
- the original/current user request and explicit non-regression constraints;
- existing focused/integration/end-to-end tests that represent real contracts;
- prior accepted runtime/field evidence, runbooks, examples, bug history, and compatibility promises;
- observable behavior at interfaces touched by the diff.
For each protected behavior record: entrypoint, input/state, expected observable result, owning contract/test, proof level, and why the current change could affect it.
Do not assume every existing test is a valuable contract. Do not let deleting or rewriting a test silently delete an accepted behavior.

3. TRACE CHANGE IMPACT THROUGH CALL STACKS
Inspect the changed symbols/files and map practical affected paths:
ENTRYPOINT -> CALLER -> ORCHESTRATION -> DOMAIN/STATE OWNER -> ADAPTER/IO -> RESULT/ERROR.
Include reverse callers and shared dependencies, schema/config migrations, caches/state, retries/cleanup, privilege/context, serialization, and concurrency only when the diff can reach them.
Use this map to select regressions. Do not run an enormous unrelated suite as a substitute for understanding impact.

4. BASELINE WHEN IT ADDS SIGNAL
When safe and affordable, exercise representative protected controls on the known-good reference in an isolated worktree/build/runtime and record the result. Then run the same controls on the candidate.
If baseline execution is impractical, use durable prior evidence and current contract tests, clearly marking the lower proof level. Never pretend a historical green badge is a fresh live baseline.

5. RUN AUTOMATED REGRESSIONS
Run in dependency-aware order:
- focused tests for the changed behavior;
- focused protected controls for impacted existing behavior;
- caller/integration tests across changed seams;
- migration/upgrade/retry/idempotency tests where the change affects persisted or transitional state;
- broader suite/build/static checks when practical.
Add a regression that reproduces every concrete regression found. Keep valid counterexamples. Do not modify expected results, snapshots, fixtures, mocks, or tolerances merely to fit the broken candidate unless the product contract truly changed and that change is explicitly supported by the request.

6. RUN THE CANONICAL LIVE PATH WHEN THE CLAIM IS LIVE
If the feature is an app/browser/service/CLI/device/operator workflow and a safe executable environment exists, do not stop at synthetic tests. Use the product's canonical launcher/entrypoint and exercise:
A. the requested new/repaired behavior; and
B. at least one impacted previously working control.
Observe the actual result, not only route issuance, command ACK, process exit, or mocked output. Collect bounded evidence/logs. If live proof requires inaccessible credentials, protected hardware/runtime, destructive action, or explicit operator authorization, state the exact gate and proof ceiling; do not claim the regression closed at the live level.

7. REPAIR WITHOUT TRADING ONE BUG FOR ANOTHER
When a protected behavior fails:
- locate the smallest canonical owner;
- preserve the requested new behavior and the old valid behavior together;
- repair implementation/contract migration rather than weakening the regression gate;
- rerun the failing control plus the new feature path immediately;
- inspect adjacent callers for the same break mechanism.
If the failure generalizes into a broader defect class, use the failure-class audit pattern; if tests bypass the real production boundary, use the production-path proof-gap pattern.

8. DELIBERATE SECOND PASS
After first green:
- inspect the diff, test changes, mocks/fixtures/snapshots, impacted call stacks, and live evidence again;
- ask `What behavior could this change break that our selected tests would not notice?`;
- add or run the smallest practical missing control;
- repeat repair/revalidation for concrete gaps.
Stop at a bounded fixed point; do not manufacture test volume.

9. AUTONOMY
Run the tests, worktrees, builds, launchers, fixtures, logs, and safe live checks yourself when tools permit. Do not make the user a regression runner or evidence courier. Escalate only a genuine inaccessible runtime/credential/physical/authorization gate.

DELIVER
Report: reference fixed point; candidate head; protected-behavior ledger; impact/call-stack map; automated regressions run; live controls run; regressions found/repaired; before/after evidence; tests added/changed; second-pass result; proof level/ceiling; remaining blocked controls; commit/PR/integration state.

ROUTING BOUNDARY
- Use failure-class auditing when one regression exposes a reusable defect class.
- Use production-path proof-gap auditing when tests and the actual execution path differ.
- Use the dedicated live-runtime executor for a deeper protected runtime proof sprint.
- Use closure certification only after preservation and requested behavior are both proved at the claimed level.
